raw_response.country: Latin America and the Caribbean (multi-country regional review covering LAC countries including Argentina, Bolivia, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Cuba, Dominican Republic, Ecuador, El Salvador, Guatemala, Haiti, Honduras, Mexico, Nicaragua, Panama, Paraguay, Peru, Uruguay, and Venezuela)

criterion_notes.c1: Although the review's primary objective is promoting wastewater and greywater reuse/reclamation to mitigate water scarcity, Sections 4 and 7.2 explicitly examine urban and rural population access to safe/healthy drinking water, sanitation inequality, and household water prices across Latin America and the Caribbean as regional context.
criterion_notes.c2: Plain vs. narrow Criterion 2 comparison: Under the plain literal wording of Criterion 2, this paper passes broadly because Section 7 (Tables 2 and 3) surveys constitutional right-to-water provisions, national water resource laws, wastewater reuse regulations, and greywater reuse legislation across LAC countries, and Section 8 briefly discusses water privatization, state management, and community management. Under the narrow 2026-10-13 rule-type mechanism reading, Criterion 2 is NOT met (no): the regulations examined in detail govern technical standards and statutory frameworks for wastewater and greywater reuse/reclamation (irrigation reuse and decentralized greywater recycling) rather than rule-type mechanisms directly governing household water or sanitation service access; the constitutional/general water law inventory and brief remarks on privatization are unanalysed macro-governance and doctrinal background; and household water prices in Figure 6 are examined only as an input to the financial payback of greywater hardware rather than as tariff or cost-recovery rules governing service access. Even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, however, the paper remains excluded (plain_criterion2_decision = exclude) because it fails Criteria 3 and 5 due to the absence of empirical access analysis or systematic empirical synthesis.
criterion_notes.c3: Published as a narrative Review, the paper combines an unsystematic Google Scholar keyword search and descriptive doctrinal/policy summaries of constitutions, water laws, and greywater bills with descriptive secondary country-level charts from FAO AQUASTAT, the World Bank, and utility tariff schedules. It contains neither primary empirical data/analysis testing how legal or governance factors affect service access nor a systematic empirical synthesis (exclude as E05).
criterion_notes.c4: Reproduces descriptive country-level secondary statistics on the percentage of total, urban, and rural populations with access to safe/healthy drinking water (Figures 3 and 5, from FAO AQUASTAT) and average household water bills for 30 m3/month consumption (Figure 6), although none of these metrics are empirically analyzed as outcomes of a legal, administrative, or governance exposure.
criterion_notes.c5: As a narrative literature and policy overview, the paper has no identifiable empirical study design evaluating a legal/regulatory exposure against an access outcome; its only bivariate charts plot country-level drinking-water coverage and water prices against GDP per capita rather than any legal, institutional, or regulatory variable.
criterion_notes.c6: Full text is written in English.

evidence_quotes.quote: Using the Aquastat database, water consumption in the world and water availability in LAC were studied. In addition, the regulatory framework for water in LAC countries was studied, with an emphasis on water reuse and greywater legislation.
In addition, the political constitution of several LAC countries was exhaustively reviewed, particularly, water laws.
The economic indicators presented in this paper were obtained from the World Bank database. The data collected from the different databases were analyzed and correlated with each other.

In Bolivia, Ecuador, Nicaragua, and Peru, between 85 and 90% of the population had access to safe drinking water, followed by the Dominican Republic which presented coverage of 84.7%, and Haiti with just 57.7% of safe drinking water access.
In LAC, only Chile has a legal norm on the specific matter of greywater, recognizing its separation from black water and therefore, from the general regulation of sanitation.
Figure 5 shows the relationship between Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita and access to healthy drinking water in some countries in Latin America.

From a regulatory point of view, most LAC countries refer to water resources in their political constitution, and more extensively, in some general water laws of each country. Similarly, each country has competent water authorities, related to a ministry or other organism.

raw_response.rationale: Excluded under E05 (No empirical evidence). This article is a narrative literature and policy/regulatory review examining water resources distribution and prospects/regulations for wastewater and greywater reuse in Latin America and the Caribbean. While it reproduces descriptive secondary country-level statistics from FAO AQUASTAT and the World Bank on urban/rural drinking-water coverage and household water bills (plotted against GDP per capita) and catalogues constitutional water provisions, general water laws, and greywater reuse legislation across LAC, it conducts neither primary empirical analysis linking any legal, administrative, or governance mechanism to water/sanitation service access nor a systematic empirical synthesis. It also fails the narrow 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 reading because its regulatory analysis centers on wastewater/greywater reuse standards and unanalysed constitutional/macro-governance background rather than rule-type mechanisms governing household service access; even under the plain wording of Criterion 2, it remains excluded for lack of empirical access evidence and an identifiable exposure-outcome study design.
raw_response.study_design: Narrative literature and regulatory/policy review with descriptive secondary country-level statistics
